title: Multi-hop cache shard scaling & network amplification — Brizo Systems technical deep dive
next_steps: Share lab benchmark script and results CSV
Schedule on-prem pilot hardware run (week of Mar 8)
Send security/KMS and private deployment docs
Propose pilot config and cost estimate
action_items: Ethan Ross: produce kv-shard profiling script and post to shared drive by 2027-02-22
Sana Ali: provide VPC topology diagram and current TLS/cipher constraints by 2027-02-24
Maya Patel: send pilot contract template and pricing options by 2027-02-25
summary: SE-led investigation of p95/p99 amplification linked to multi-hop edge proxies and hot cache shard evictions. Discussed streaming vs non-streaming paths, quantization tradeoffs, and on-prem/VPC constraints. Agreed on lab benchmarks, KV profiling, and an on-prem pilot run.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-02-17 14:30 UTC - Duration approx 78 minutes - Attendees: Maya, Ethan (Redwood); Liam, Sana, Marco (Brizo)

[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining on time uh we got about an hour and change, um wanted to tee up the agenda quick — Ethan will run through the traces and we can dig into the hot shard behavior.
[00:18] Liam O'Connor: yeah thanks, we have two objectives: one is understand root cause of the p99 spikes hitting our customer-facing endpoints, second is evaluate whether Redwood Dedicated or Private on-prem makes sense for us given compliance.
[00:32] Ethan Ross: cool — quick note i pulled the end-to-end traces you sent last week and correlated them with the KV cache metrics, so i'll share screen in a sec, um if the recording messes up sorry in advance.
[00:46] Sana Ali: quick context — Brizo runs a multi-region edge proxy in front of our inference fleet; requests sometimes hop through an edge proxy, then a regional proxy, then the inference node. average path is 2 hops but p99 paths had 4-5 hops.
[01:05] Marco Ruiz: and we have a small fleet of NVLink-connected hosts on prem for some customers; rest is cloud VPC. we started seeing 95th and 99th latency drift after we rolled quantized 8-bit weights last month.
[01:25] Ethan Ross: okay makes sense — two obvious signals: network path length (multi-hop amplification) and cache eviction-induced cold KVs. i'll walk through a trace snippet where both coincide.
[01:45] [screen noise, faint typing]
[02:12] Ethan Ross: here — this trace from feb 5th shows a request enters edge-us, gets proxied to edge-eu, then to regional-eu, then to inference node. the inter-proxy latency is small generally but when a cache miss triggers remote KV fetch, you add 60-120ms per hop in worst cases.
[02:38] Liam O'Connor: are those additional latencies coming from TCP handshake or from serialization/deserialize on the proxy?
[02:46] Ethan Ross: a bit of both, but mostly serialization + small thread queuing on the proxy side — we also saw occasional TLS renegotiation on older proxies which adds spikes.
[02:58] Sana Ali: oh that TLS renegotiation — we disabled keepalive on one of the proxy pools as a mitigation earlier, maybe that contributed.
[03:08] Maya Patel: helpful — thanks. quick clarifying question: when you say cache miss triggers remote KV fetch is that the model kv or a prefix-level cache?
[03:18] Ethan Ross: model KV cache — the per-shard KV cache that we keep pinned memory for, so ideally a prefix hit gives you local access. but when a shard's working set grows, we start evicting into an LRU that's backed by the remote store which needs a network call.
[03:32] Marco Ruiz: and that remote store is S3-like object store with a small retrieval lib we wrote. not super fast.
[03:40] Ethan Ross: yep, so two problems collide: 1) hot shard gets evicted under sudden RPS, 2) requests route through an extra proxy layer, multiply the extra remote fetch latency. that's the amplification.
[03:58] [00:04:10] Liam O'Connor: does Redwood's runtime provide async prefetching or cache warmers to avoid these misses?
[04:10] Ethan Ross: we do have a prefetch/warming daemon in the runtime — it works well when patterns are predictable. but when you have highly tail-y traffic (rare queries that touch deep KV keys) the warming isn't perfect; we can tune the prefetch policy and threshold by workload.
[04:28] Sana Ali: what about streaming vs non-streaming generation — we've seen that switching to streaming reduced avg latency but increased tail because streaming keeps more open channels across proxies.
[04:40] Ethan Ross: correct — streaming reduces perceived latency to the user through early tokens, but it changes connection life-time and backpressure behavior. with prolonged open streams, proxies can queue other traffic or hit connection limits and create head-of-line effects.
[04:58] Marco Ruiz: that was our hypothesis — the p95 looked great with streaming but p99 got worse. is there a recommended hybrid?
[05:06] Ethan Ross: often we recommend a hybrid: streaming for short responses (< 128 tokens) and non-streaming for long completions, or use early flush thresholds on the server to close streams after prefix tokens. also consider isolating streaming traffic onto dedicated proxy pool to avoid contention.
[05:26] Maya Patel: okay some quick ops questions — on the quantization point, you mentioned 8-bit rollout correlated with increased tail. what's the mechanism?
[05:36] Ethan Ross: two subtle things: int8 kernels can be slightly slower for small batch sizes on some GPU drivers because dequant/quant transforms add per-token overhead; and more importantly, low-precision kernels often change memory access pattern for KV cache shaping — we saw a case where int8 layout increased KV footprint for certain families, leading to more evictions.
[05:56] Sana Ali: hmm we did see a larger footprint in memory charts. we assumed it was smaller with 8-bit but maybe layout overhead or alignment padded it.
[06:04] Ethan Ross: exactly — padding can blow up small shards. also fallback paths matter: when the runtime falls back to a slower reference kernel on a node, that single request can add tens to hundreds ms and create a tail.
[06:18] Liam O'Connor: can we force model variant routing so that sensitive endpoints always go to a non-quantized model?
[06:26] Ethan Ross: yes — Redwood supports routing policies by model variant and by customer tag. We can route high-SLA endpoints to a float16 variant on Dedicated capacity while routing best-effort to quantized variants.
[06:40] [06:40] Marco Ruiz: from infra cost point, Dedicated will be more expensive but gives predictability. Private on-prem gives us data control but then we have to operate the runtime.
[06:54] Maya Patel: right — we'll include comparative numbers in the follow-up. Ethan, can you show the KV op timeline for a single hot spike?
[07:03] Ethan Ross: sure — (shares trace) here's a 30s window: you can see repeated get_kv ops, eviction at t+4s, then remote fetch at t+6s, then a bunch of queued requests waiting. the p99 aligns with a few requests that hit remote store and also got extra hop via the standby proxy.
[07:30] Sana Ali: on the remote store fetch, would it help to have a local SSD-backed tier or a compacted KV shard snapshot on the proxies?
[07:40] Ethan Ross: both are valid — SSD local tier on inference nodes is fastest. alternatively, we can push a compacted hotset snapshot to proxies — that reduces remote fetches but increases proxied storage and sync complexity.
[07:56] Liam O'Connor: any recommendations for shard size and eviction policy to reduce thrash?
[08:04] Ethan Ross: we often tune to smaller shard sizes when you have skewed hot keys — smaller shards reduce blast radius but increase cross-shard fetches; for eviction, a segmented LRU with admission control helped other customers.
[08:20] Marco Ruiz: segmented LRU — is that in the open runtime config or a proprietary module?
[08:28] Ethan Ross: it's an option in Redwood's runtime config; we can toggle admission parameters. i'll push the exact config snippet.
[08:36] [08:36] Speaker 1: {laughs} the config we got last time was a little dense.
[08:40] Maya Patel: noted, we'll make it clearer. quick question — for VPC/on-prem, we saw earlier you had KMS integrations — is HSM supported?
[08:50] Ethan Ross: yes for Private deployments we can integrate with customer HSMs; for hosted we support cloud KMS options and bring-your-own-key via customer-managed keys.
[08:59] Sana Ali: that is important for PCI/sensitive customers.
[09:04] Liam O'Connor: back to the network — you mentioned proxy TLS renegotiation, is the solution to upgrade proxies or tune keepalive?
[09:12] Ethan Ross: both — keepalive tuning reduces renegotiation; upgrading proxies to use session resumption avoids full handshake at scale. Putting long-lived streams on dedicated pools also helps.
[09:24] Marco Ruiz: I'm worried about connection limits though — our proxies start dropping long streams under load.
[09:31] Ethan Ross: then we should partition streaming traffic: either dedicate proxies or use a connection proxy tier with larger ulimit and optimized epoll settings. also consider using HTTP/2 multiplexing or gRPC to reduce per-connection overhead.
[09:48] Sana Ali: do you have a recommended benchmark we should run in our lab to reproduce the p99?
[09:55] Ethan Ross: yes — i'll share a bench script that mimics your traffic distribution, including tail-heavy rare keys, and a KV misalignment scenario. it will run three modes: streaming-only, non-streaming-only, hybrid with dedicated proxy pool.
[10:12] Maya Patel: great. we'll include that in the next-steps.
[10:18] [10:18] Liam O'Connor: what about model fallbacks — can the routing automatically fallback to smaller models when a node is overloaded?
[10:26] Ethan Ross: Redwood supports automatic fallback policies by latency/cpu pressure; you can specify fallback to a compatible model family or degrade output length. but watch quality drift — we'll tie in eval suites to detect regressions.
[10:40] Marco Ruiz: thinking operationally, if we do on-prem, we need clear runbooks for cache priming and shard resync during node restarts.
[10:50] Ethan Ross: understood — we provide runbooks and an optional managed services add-on where Redwood helpers run the initial pilots and handover.
[11:00] Sana Ali: curious about quantization-mode: can we run mixed-precision per-layer to reduce footprint without changing layout radically?
[11:08] Ethan Ross: yes mixed precision or per-layer quantization narrows footprint growth. Another approach is block-wise quantization that keeps KV layout closer to fp16. We can model this in a short benchmark.
[11:22] [11:22] Liam O'Connor: do you track model-level p99 separately from network p99 in instrumented traces?
[11:30] Ethan Ross: we do — Redwood's console decomposes token-level latency into model execution, kv fetch, kernel fallback, and network hops. that decomposition helped us attribute spikes in these traces.
[11:44] Marco Ruiz: helpful — could you show a console screenshot of the decomposition?
[11:48] Ethan Ross: shared in chat: https://redwood.app/shared/brizo-decomp-2027-02-17.png (see network hop bars).
[11:58] Sana Ali: nice. i see a large yellow band labeled 'remote_kv_fetch'.
[12:04] Ethan Ross: correct. that yellow band correlates with proxy hop counts in the other metric.
[12:10] [12:10] Maya Patel: let's get tactical for the pilot: propose 3-track approach: 1) lab replay of production traces with bench script, 2) Dedicated capacity test in cloud region to validate routing + prefetch tuning, 3) small on-prem pilot to validate KMS and network topology.
[12:26] Liam O'Connor: sounds good. timeline?
[12:30] Maya Patel: bench script shared by Feb 22, run week of Mar 1, Dedicated test week of Mar 8, on-prem pilot week of Mar 15 (tentative).
[12:40] Marco Ruiz: ok. for the on-prem pilot we'll need a test cluster spec — CPU, GPU, NVMe sizes.
[12:48] Ethan Ross: i'll include recommended specs in the follow-up doc including kernel/driver versions for optimal int8 kernels.
[12:58] Sana Ali: a question about rate-limiting and throttles — we currently apply simple token bucket per-customer which sometimes causes bursting across shards. any better pattern?
[13:08] Ethan Ross: consider token buckets per logical route and circuit breakers at proxy layer; plus smoothing at ingress with small queueing windows to flatten bursts. also adaptive admission to reject low-priority requests when a shard is hot.
[13:26] Liam O'Connor: sounds reasonable. can the runtime emit signals for shard hotness to adjust upstream admission?
[13:34] Ethan Ross: yes we can emit hot-shard metrics and integrate with upstream rate-limiter to throttle routes touching a hot shard.
[13:44] [13:44] Speaker 2: side comment — last month we saw a single key generate 30% of traffic, maybe we should shard by key hash differently.
[13:54] Ethan Ross: re-sharding by hash salt or dynamic hot-shard splitting are both options; dynamic splitting is more complex but reduces manual work.
[14:06] Marco Ruiz: what's the typical operator overhead for dynamic splitting?
[14:12] Ethan Ross: with our tooling it's moderate — we provide scripts and a controller; still requires validation and some ops time during the initial period.
[14:25] Maya Patel: ok we're about 14 minutes in, want to switch to bench output that Maya uploaded earlier?
[14:33] Ethan Ross: sure — (shows bench) this lab run simulates your tail distribution; you can see p95 at ~120ms in baseline, p99 spiking to 400ms when we introduced a hot shard evictions plus an extra proxy hop.
[14:55] Liam O'Connor: that matches what we saw. can you break down the 400ms?
[15:01] Ethan Ross: roughly 80ms model exec, 70ms kernel fallback jitter, 160ms remote_kv_fetch (including two hop delays), 60ms queuing.
[15:14] Sana Ali: interesting — kernel fallback jitter is non-trivial. can we pin nodes to avoid falling back?
[15:22] Ethan Ross: yes pinning to nodes with known-good drivers and using node labels for variant routing reduces fallback incidence. Also pre-warming the kernels avoids cold starts.
[15:32] Marco Ruiz: what's the cost delta for pinning versus letting scheduler bin-pack?
[15:38] Ethan Ross: depends on utilization — pinning increases headroom and may raise cost by 10-25% for the pinned pool, but gives predictable latency. we can model exact numbers for your utilization.
[15:50] [15:50] Liam O'Connor: one last question before we move to recaps — are there any quick wins we should try within a week?
[15:58] Ethan Ross: yes three quick wins: 1) tune keepalive/session resumption on proxy pools, 2) increase local SSD tier for hotset on inference nodes, 3) route streaming traffic to a dedicated proxy pool. these are low-effort and high-probability to reduce tails.
[16:18] Maya Patel: perfect. we'll capture those in the follow-up.
[16:24] [01:17:30] Maya Patel: ok wrapping up — recap: Ethan to share bench script and config, Sana to share topology and constraints, Maya to send pilot and pricing; next meeting planned after initial lab results. we'll also include a link to the console decomposition and the kv profiling script.
[01:17:58] Liam O'Connor: thanks all — look forward to the bench results and I'll coordinate internal stakeholders.
[01:18:05] Maya Patel: thanks everyone.

References and shared artifacts: https://redwood.app/shared/brizo-decomp-2027-02-17.png ; bench script: https://redwood.app/shared/brizo-bench-2027.sh ; lab results placeholder: https://redwood.app/shared/brizo-lab-2027.csv

Transcript notes: transcription contains minor speaker mislabels and occasional mishears (TLS renegotiation sometimes transcribed as 'TLS re-neg') — treat timestamps as approximate.
